Series::max¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::max() const -> Series
Series::max(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::max(std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim) const -> Series
Series::max(const Series& other) const -> Series

What It Does¶

max() is one of the few Series methods whose meaning changes materially with the overload you choose.

  • max() with no arguments is a full ordered reduction

  • max(dim, keepdim) is an ordered reduction along one axis

  • max(other) is not a reduction at all; it is an elementwise comparison

That split matters because the shape rules, autograd behavior, and even the mental model are different.

If you want “the largest value inside this series,” stay on the reduction overloads. If you want “compare this series against another one position by position,” the binary overload is the right surface.

Overload Map¶

max()

Reduces across every element and returns one scalar Series.

max(dim)

Reduces along one axis and removes that axis from the result.

max(dim, keepdim)

Reduces along one axis and optionally preserves that axis as size 1.

max(other)

Returns the elementwise winner between self and other under broadcasting. Numerically, this is the same job as maximum().

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis to reduce for the reduction overloads.

  • positive dims count from the front

  • negative dims count from the back

  • the dim must refer to an existing axis

keepdim (bool)

Whether the reduced axis is retained as size 1.

  • false: the axis disappears

  • true: the axis stays, which is often more convenient if the result will be broadcast back against the original shape

other (const Series&)

The peer operand for the binary overload.

  • other is broadcast against self

  • the result shape is the broadcasted shape, not a reduced shape

  • this overload has no scalar sibling; if the other side is a scalar, the clearer surface is maximum()

Returns¶

Series A scalar, a reduced series, or a broadcasted comparison result depending on the overload.

Gradient¶

The autograd story depends on the overload family.

Reduction Overloads¶

For max(), max(dim), and max(dim, keepdim):

  • only winning values receive sensitivity

  • if a reduced lane has multiple equal maxima, the incoming derivative is split evenly across those ties

  • for full reduction, the split is across every global maximum, not just within one intermediate axis-wise step

That last point is worth being explicit about because it is exactly what users normally expect from a full extrema reduction.

Binary Overload¶

For max(other):

  • the backward rule is the same as maximum()

  • gradient flows to self where self >= other

  • gradient flows to other where self < other

  • at an exact tie, the full gradient goes to self

So the reduction overloads split ties, while the binary overload does not. Those are different operations that happen to share one public name.

Examples¶

The examples on this page build incrementally.

Example 1. With no arguments, max() collapses the whole series to one scalar winner.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 7.0, 3.0},
    {4.0, 7.0, 6.0},
});

std::cout << scores.max();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=7

This is a true reduction result: one 0-D Series, not a row or column.

Example 2. max(dim) reduces one axis instead of the whole object.

std::cout << scores.max(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[7, 7]

Here dim = 1 means “reduce across columns,” so each row contributes one winner.

Example 3. keepdim=true keeps the reduced axis available for later broadcasting.

std::cout << scores.max(1, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[7],
  [7]]

This is the same value result as Example 2, but with a shape that still remembers where the reduction happened.

Example 4. Negative dims are normalized from the back.

std::cout << scores.max(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[7, 7]

For a rank-2 series, -1 means the last axis, so this is the same reduction as max(1).

Example 5. The binary overload is an elementwise comparison, not a reduction.

auto floor_by_column = pluss::make_series({2.0, 6.0, 8.0});

std::cout << scores.max(floor_by_column);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[2, 7, 8],
  [4, 7, 8]]

Every row of scores is compared against the same [2, 6, 8] peer under ordinary broadcasting. No axis disappears because nothing is being reduced.

Example 6. max(other) is numerically the same operation as maximum(other).

std::cout << scores.maximum(floor_by_column);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[2, 7, 8],
  [4, 7, 8]]

This is why it helps to think of max(other) as a compatibility-style spelling that lands on the same comparison family as maximum().

Example 7. On a dimension reduction, ties split the derivative across the winning lane.

auto reduced_ties = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 5.0, 5.0},
    {2.0, -1.0, 2.0},
});
reduced_ties.tracks_slope_(true);

auto reduced_winners = reduced_ties.max(1);
reduced_winners.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << reduced_winners << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << reduced_ties.sensitivity();

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 2]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 0.5, 0.5],
  [0.5, 0, 0.5]]

The first row has two equal winners (5 and 5), so that row’s unit upstream derivative becomes 0.5 and 0.5. The second row does the same thing across its tied 2s.

Example 8. Full reduction also splits evenly across every global winner.

auto global_ties = pluss::make_series({
    {7.0, 0.0, 0.0},
    {7.0, 7.0, 1.0},
});
global_ties.tracks_slope_(true);

auto global_winner = global_ties.max();
global_winner.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << global_winner << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << global_ties.sensitivity();

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=7
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.33333333, 0, 0],
  [0.33333333, 0.33333333, 0]]

There are three global maxima, so each receives one third of the derivative. This is the behavior you usually want from a true full reduction.

Example 9. The binary overload does not split ties; exact equality still attributes the derivative to self.

auto lhs = pluss::make_series({1.0, 5.0, 2.0});
auto rhs = pluss::make_series({4.0, 2.0, 2.0});
lhs.tracks_slope_(true);
rhs.tracks_slope_(true);

auto binary = lhs.max(rhs);
binary.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << binary << "\n";
std::cout << "dlhs=" << lhs.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "drhs=" << rhs.sensitivity();

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 5, 2]
dlhs=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 1]
drhs=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0, 0]

Index 2 is the boundary case: both values are 2, but the derivative still belongs entirely to lhs because the binary rule uses the inclusive self >= other boundary.

Example 10. An invalid dimension fails through the shared reduction validator.

try {
  std::cout << scores.max(2) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

reduce: dim out of range

That generic message is not a typo in the docs. max(dim, ...) uses the shared reduction shape-normalization path, so the error text comes from the common reduction validator rather than a max-specific formatter.

Notes¶

  • max() is overloaded across two different ideas: ordered reduction and elementwise comparison.

  • max(other) is comparison-family behavior and is numerically equivalent to maximum(other).

  • max(other) does not have a scalar overload. For scalar thresholds or scalar-vs-series comparison, prefer maximum().

  • Ordered reduction requires an orderable dtype. Complex tensors are not valid reduction operands here.

See Also¶

  • Series::maximum: the explicit elementwise comparison spelling.

  • Series::minimum: the elementwise lower counterpart.

  • Series::sum: reduction with the same shape rules but additive rather than order-based.
